   2. Check Postmaster Tools for Nov 13–14.

Gmail tends to be cautious with first-time senders and recipients, so a low open rate on a first email to new contacts is common and usually points to deliverability rather than copy.

- **Sender reputation and engagement history:** New domains and IPs have no track record, so initial emails to new recipients often go to spam. Gmail relies heavily on user engagement to determine inbox placement.
- **Authentication:** Insufficient SPF, DKIM, or DMARC setup is listed as a contributing factor for first emails landing in spam (source 4-3).
- **List quality:** Emails sent to invalid addresses bounce, and a bounce rate above 2% signals to email providers that you're not maintaining a clean list.

- **Engagement tactics:** Asking recipients to add you to their contacts or reply can signal positive engagement to Gmail (source 4-6).

Sources disagree on emphasis. Even from the sender that reaches Gmail's Primary tab, batch 2 is at 22.6%. Earlier campaigns from that same sender reached 33–56%. So the sender change alone doesn't close the gap.

I matched production data against who opened, with emails hashed inside the page. Of the 547 JusPrin 1 users who chatted since Sep 19, only 18 have ever had an Obico printer. That's 3%, so almost none of them get Obico's printer notification emails. They have little reason to recognise or open mail from obico.io.

- The JusPrin 1.4.0 email in Oct 2025 got 41.6% from early JusPrin users. About a quarter of them had Obico printers.
- In batch 1, the 10 printer owners opened at 60% even from the new sender. Everyone else opened at 13%.

Gmail also started sorting the Promotions tab by how much each person engages with the sender. Mail to Obico's printer users didn't visibly suffer from this in Feb and Apr 2026. People with no history with obico.io may be hit harder.

**One thing I checked and set aside:** almost all batch contacts were created in SendGrid on Nov 12. That looked like proof they'd never been emailed. But 35,000 of the 47,000 contacts on the TSD list were also created that day, and old open history is gone, so contacts were deleted and re-added at some point. It tells us nothing about these people.

**Still unproven:** the audience explanation rests on a small printer-owner sample. There's no recent campaign from support@ to non-Obico users to compare against. Clicks are too few to compare: 1 and 2.

content.text:
Yes. One batch can test the subject line and the sender name, and also show whether people's history with Obico matters. About 6,000 JusPrin 1 users haven't been emailed yet, and 79% of them use Gmail. That's enough people to answer all of this in one send.

**First, a correction.** I proposed splitting people by whether SendGrid had held them as contacts since Feb 2026. Only 8 of the 6,000 qualify, so that split won't work. Production data gives a better one. About 1,000 of the 6,000 have an Obico printer, so they already get mail from obico.io. About 3,900 started using JusPrin before mid-October 2025, so they were probably on the list for the JusPrin 1.3.0 and 1.4.0 emails. I haven't checked who actually received those.

**The four explanations I think are most likely**

1. People with no history with obico.io open less. This is my strongest suspect.
2. The display name "Obi The Owl" versus a person's name. The address (support@obico.io) is already settled. The name isn't tested.
3. The subject line. "Free with your own API key" may read as an ad, and "API key" may mean nothing to many users.
4. Opens are undercounting real readers. Gmail loads fewer tracking images now, so opens may miss people who did read the email.

**Proposed experiment for batch 3 (not approved, nothing built)**

- **Who gets it:** about 2,400 randomly chosen people from the 6,000. That leaves about 3,600 to receive whichever version wins.
- **Same for everyone:** sent from support@obico.io, all at the same minute.
- **Split by subject:** half get the current subject. The other half get a plainer one, such as "JusPrin 2 is here". You'd choose the exact wording.
- **Split by sender name:** independently, half see "Obi The Owl" and half see "Kenneth from JusPrin". So there are four combinations, with about 600 people each.
- **Balanced history:** the split is drawn so that printer owners, early JusPrin users and newer users are spread evenly across all four combinations.

What this answers:
- **Subject:** 1,200 people against 1,200. That's enough to see a gap of about 5 points.
- **Sender name:** the same comparison, using the other split.
- **History:** printer owners against everyone else, compared in all four combinations together. The cleanest comparison is among early users who last chatted in 2025: about 850 with printers and about 2,800 without. If my strongest suspect is right, printer owners should open roughly twice as often.
- **Undercounting:** I'd also count, from production, who creates a JusPrin 2 account within 7 days. If one subject wins on opens but not on sign-ups, the open counts are misleading.

Two tests are left out on purpose:
- **Send time:** held fixed so it doesn't muddy the rest.
- **Hotmail and Outlook spam:** a separate problem that affects about 10% of each batch.

Setting it up in SendGrid takes four segments built from a new field marking each person's version, plus four campaigns scheduled for the same minute. "Kenneth from JusPrin" sending from support@obico.io would be a new sender in SendGrid, and it has to be verified before it can send.

**Decision needed: how big should batch 3's test be?**

- **The full test above (my pick):** subject line and sender name together, about 2,400 people. It answers the most questions in one send. It needs one more SendGrid sender and four campaigns.
- **Subject line only:** about 1,200 people, everything sent as "Obi The Owl". Simpler to set up, but it says nothing about using your name.
- **Neither:** send everyone the batch 2 version. No new setup, but nothing new learned.

input.ask: Should we spend about $59 on a GlockApps month to test SES against SendGrid on test inboxes?

content.text:
Yes. At the start I suspected SendGrid's shared sending servers, because SpamCop lists one of them as a spam source. The seed test since then shows SendGrid isn't the problem for Gmail, Yahoo or AOL. It's still a suspect for Hotmail, Outlook and iCloud. A split test with SES makes sense, but I'd run it on test inboxes first, not on real recipients.

**What the evidence shows**

The test copy from support@obico.io went through SendGrid's shared servers like everything else. It still landed in Gmail's Primary tab in all 22 Gmail inboxes. Yahoo had it in the inbox 8 of 8 times, and AOL 7 of 8. Whatever is wrong with SendGrid, it isn't hurting those providers.

Microsoft and Apple look different. Of 13 Hotmail and Outlook test inboxes, 5 put the email in Spam and 8 never received it. iCloud never received it in any of its 3. That held for both sender addresses, so it points at something shared by both copies: the sending servers, or the obico.io domain itself. Real recipients match this. Microsoft users opened 2 of 33 batch 1 emails and 1 of 18 batch 2 emails, and iCloud users opened 0 of 4. Those providers are about 12% of each batch. Even a full fix there would raise the overall open rate by only about 2 points.

**SES is already set up for obico.io**

Obico's server mail, such as the "We couldn't charge your Card" emails from admin@obico.io, already goes through Amazon SES. Gmail shows it passing both domain checks under obico.io's name. So a test send through SES needs no new DNS setup.

**Why not test it on real recipients yet**

- **Building:** SendGrid gives us the unsubscribe link, the one-click unsubscribe header, and open and click counts. SES gives us none of that ready-made. We'd have to build an unsubscribe that also updates SendGrid's unsubscribe group, plus open and click tracking.
- **Risk:** SES pauses a whole account if spam complaints pass 0.1% or bounces pass 5%. Batch 1 bounced 2.3%. A pause would also stop Obico's billing and alert emails, which share the same SES account.

**My proposal**

Repeat the seed test through both services: the same email from support@obico.io, sent once through SendGrid and once through SES, to the GlockApps test inboxes. If SES gets into Hotmail, Outlook and iCloud inboxes where SendGrid doesn't, a real-recipient split becomes worth the building work and the risk. If both fail the same way, the cause is the domain or the content, and switching services won't help.

**Decision needed:** our free GlockApps tests are used up. This one needs a paid month, which third-party reviews put at about $59, though sources disagree. The same month would also let us check the subject line and the "Kenneth from JusPrin" name on test inboxes before batch 3 goes to real people. The free alternative is a few real Outlook and iCloud inboxes that you or the team already own. That's cheaper, but those inboxes have history with you, so they're a weaker test. My pick is the paid month.

Yes. The original list had nine possible causes. Batch 3 tests two of them by random split. It also answers two more without a split, because they can be read across all four groups. Three are already settled, and two are left out.

**Settled before batch 3**
- **Sender address:** jusprin-support@obico.io landed in Gmail's Promotions tab in the seed test, while support@obico.io landed in Primary. Real opens agree, so batch 3 uses support@obico.io for every group.
- **One-click unsubscribe:** the campaign email already has the header. Postmaster's warning is about Obico's own server mail.
- **Apple Mail opening emails automatically:** that would inflate opens, not lower them. The drop is inside Gmail, so it doesn't explain anything.

**Tested in batch 3 by random split**
- The subject line.
- The sender name, "Obi The Owl" or "Kenneth from JusPrin".

**Answered in batch 3 without a split**
- **History with obico.io:** we can't randomly give people an Obico printer, so this is read by comparing printer owners, early JusPrin users and newer users across all four groups. Each group gets an even share of each kind of person.
- **Opens undercounting real readers:** JusPrin 2 sign-ups within 7 days are counted alongside opens, so a subject that only wins on opens won't be picked.

**Left out**
- **Send time:** held at one minute for everyone, so it can't muddy the other results.
- **Language:** the email is in English. The idea that recipients are mostly Brazilian was never checked. A translated version needs the translation, plus a way to know each person's language, and we have neither.
- **SendGrid against Amazon SES:** you said not now.

Adding a third factor costs less than it sounds, because each comparison still uses everyone. With send time added, batch 3 becomes eight groups of about 300. The subject comparison is still 1,200 against 1,200, and so are sender name and send time. Each can still detect a difference of about 4–5 points. The costs are eight campaigns and segments instead of four, and the cross-effects become harder to read. The interaction between subject and sender name is already only a hint at this size.

**Decision needed: should send time be the third factor?**

- **Add send time (my pick):** half of batch 3 goes out at one time and half at another, for example 7 AM and 5 PM Pacific on the same weekday. We don't know where recipients live, so the answer is which Pacific time works for this mixed audience. That's the clock time we'd use for the remaining 3,600 people anyway. It costs four more campaigns and segments, which I'd build.
- **Keep two factors:** four groups, all at one time. Simpler, and send time stays untested.
- **Add language instead:** I'd only do this after checking whether production records each person's language or country. Without that, we'd be guessing who should get the translated email.

If we believe that a printer history is the most important factor, shouldn't we make sure that they are evenly distributed across the four splits so that we don't have a biased unbalanced data set coming back?

Yes, "JusPrin 2 is here" was my stand-in. When I proposed the test, the only reason I gave was that it was "a plainer one" than the current subject, and I said you'd choose the exact wording. So the result is real but narrow. It shows the stand-in beat "JusPrin 2: open source AI slicer, free with your own API key" (28.5% against 24.1% opened, unlikely to be chance). It doesn't show why, and it doesn't show the stand-in is a good subject. It only tells us the current one is worse.

The two subjects differ in several ways at once, so each of these is still only a hypothesis:

1. **Length.** The stand-in is 17 characters and the current one is 59. On a phone, the inbox list shows roughly the first 35–40 characters, so people saw "JusPrin 2: open source AI slicer, fr…". The cut hides the part meant to persuade.
2. **It reads like an ad.** "Free", "AI" and a feature pitch look like marketing. A short "X is here" looks like news from a product you already use. It could also change whether Gmail files the email under Promotions, but Gmail decides that mostly by sender, so I'd rank this low.
3. **"API key" puts people off.** To someone who has never made an API key, "free with your own API key" sounds like setup work, or like "not really free".
4. **It's news people half-expected.** Everyone in this batch used JusPrin 1, so "JusPrin 2 is here" answers something they already know about. If this is the reason, the lift should be biggest among early JusPrin 1 users and smallest among recent sign-ups.
5. **It sounds like a note from the maker.** The new subject gained 8 points from "Kenneth from JusPrin" and almost nothing from "Obi The Owl". A short subject with a person's name may read as a personal message. But this rests on one group of about 560 people, and our decision rule treats it as a hint only.

We can check hypothesis 4 with data we already have, at no cost. I'd split each group's openers by early versus newer JusPrin 1 users, and by printer owners, using the same hashed production data we balanced the groups with. I'd fold this into tomorrow's 48-hour read, which already planned to split by history. Hypotheses 1, 2, 3 and 5 can only be separated by new subjects.

**Proposal, not agreed:** don't send the winner to all of the roughly 3,600 people left. Instead, run one more round that pulls these explanations apart. All three versions would come from "Kenneth from JusPrin":
- "JusPrin 2 is here", as the baseline.
- A short subject with one benefit and no "free" or "API key", for example "JusPrin 2 is here: AI that fixes failed prints". If this beats the baseline, the pitch was never the problem; the length and the API-key wording were.
- A short, personal subject, for example "I rebuilt JusPrin". If this wins, the personal-note explanation gains ground.

Decision needed: should we spend the remaining people on a three-subject test, or send the winner to everyone? Three versions at about 1,200 each would use all 3,600 people. That leaves nobody to receive the final winner, but it can detect a gap of about 4–5 points, and later announcements to other lists would benefit. Sending "JusPrin 2 is here" to all 3,600 gets the best known version out now, but teaches us nothing more. A middle path is two versions at about 1,200 each, with the remaining 1,200 getting the winner. That middle path is my pick, because it keeps a real test and still sends the best subject to a third of the people. Which way do you want to go, and do you want to write the subjects yourself?
What were all the hypotheses that we were targeting batch 3 for? and come up with a clear conclusion on all of them. The conclusion can be validated, invalidated, or need further investigation.

content.text:
I read batch 3 at about 47.5 hours after the send, which counts as the 48-hour read. That makes the 10:23 check redundant, so I cancelled it.

Batch 3 was built to test four hypotheses. Here's where each one landed:

1. **Subject line: confirmed.** "JusPrin 2 is here" got 31.0% of people to open, against 25.8% for the current subject. The gap is too large to be likely chance (p = 0.006), so by the rule we fixed before sending, it wins. Most of the gain came from people who started using JusPrin 1 early. Among newer users, the gain was small enough to be chance. That fits the idea that it works because people already knew JusPrin 2 was coming. That reading is still only a hint, not a result.

2. **Sender name: no measured difference.** "Kenneth from JusPrin" got 29.2% and "Obi The Owl" got 27.7%, which could easily be chance. Under our rule, that means you choose. There's one hint: with the new subject, your name did better (33.3% against 28.8%). That's not strong enough to count as a result.

3. **People with no history with obico.io open less: confirmed.** People with an Obico printer opened 37.8% of the time, against 24.4% for everyone else. People who joined JusPrin 1 early, and so got the old JusPrin 1.3 and 1.4 emails, opened no more than newer users. So it's the regular Obico printer emails that build the habit of opening mail from obico.io, not the old JusPrin emails. This is a correlation, not a random split. Printer owners may also be more engaged in general.

4. **Opens miss real readers: confirmed, but small.** 5 of the 32 people who clicked a link, and 2 of the 9 who made a JusPrin 2 account, never showed up as an open. So opens miss about 1 in 5 engaged readers. It shouldn't change any of the comparisons above. The email itself does drive sign-ups: 9 accounts from the 2,414 people emailed, and none from the 3,618 we held back (p < 0.001). Sign-ups are still too few to judge the subject or the sender by: 5 against 4. The Nov 21 read may add a few more.

One new finding: the weak step is clicking, not opening. About 28% opened but only 1.4% clicked a link, and that held for both subjects. Better subject lines won't fix that. The email body and its button are the next things to test.

The verdicts and per-campaign numbers are in `jusprin2-batch1-low-opens.md` in the shared notes folder. The 3,618 people not yet emailed should get "JusPrin 2 is here". Which sender name to use is the choice the box below asks you.
